review:
[H1]Pros:[/h1]

+ Responsive roguelite adventure game, with base building that is interesting (despite having some flaws). Your character's ability to dodge cancel is a godsend, and every swing of your sword or shot of a curse feels weighty. 

+ One of the most well crafted and executed visual styles in an indie game I've played to date. The game weaves a mix of cartoonish cutesy and eldritch horror in everything - the scenary, characters, and monsters especially. You can't help but smile at everyone's expressive reactions, or the cute way they 'talk'. Also, Cult of the Lamb's Interface design, and overall design style, is sharp and responsive as well, with no fat whatsoever. 

+ Some pretty solid writing and world building, between the five brothers and the gods they have become. Crows will convey some deeper details if you're curious for them, and creatures of all walks of life and sizes will talk about your journey.

+ Solid music that leaves an impression and changes depending on the stage. I loved the base theme, in particular, which had a nice carefree vibe that paired well with the vibe of cutesy animals working hard or doing horrible things.

+ Customization and base building are HUGE focuses that are very fun to involve yourself in. Your cult's name, your follower's names and forms, the way they interact with each other - you have a great degree of control over these things, and it can be fun to mess with this for quite awhile. 

+ There are multiple difficulty options to choose from, making the game very accessible. On normal, I clocked a solid playtime of around 22 hours. I could easily see most people hitting a playtime of 16-20, with more or less depending on your preference on the game.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]

- [b] Core Flaws: [/b] The game is the definition of "so close". So many of its systems (weapons, curses, cloaks, abilities, cultist perks, base building, rerun mechanics, Tarot cards) are wonderful takes on the roguelite genre that, unfortunately, are only scratching the surface of their true potential. For example, the game is plagued by the "the right choice" problem, whether its combat (where the gold cloak is objectively the best choice when compared with useless alternatives) or upgrades (Ritual of Resurrection vs Funeral, one of many bad choices). Another example is that often many of the rewards feel pointless or lackluster, including many of the Tarot cards (poison immunity when poison is so infrequent, heart upgrades that feel meaningless, etc). ANOTHER example is that base building has weird uneven terrain, or that you cannot extend your flooring to the edges of the map. And finally, perhaps the worst example -- rerunning levels is limited to only 3 runs, and has no real point of replaying them because inevitably your runs will largely look the same. You'll start to see more cracks in the game the more you play, until, inevitably, you will think "Ah, that sucks that it isn't deeper. It'd be cool if..." and get lost in thoughts about ideas. It is a crying shame how much of this game could be so much better.

- [b] Followers: [/b] I love this system, but man, they got to be incredibly annoying to manage, and it really sucked that the design philosophy around them was encouraging the player to see them as disposable. Getting attached to a follower is expensive and outright impossible, whether it's because of old age, being betrayed, or needing to use them as a resource of some kind, particularly if you want to get 100% of all follower unlocks. 

- [b] Annoying enemy design: [/b] Often the only thing that ever hurt me was the smaller enemies that are unpredictable, usually because the dense foliage hid them from my sight. The first stage is still my least favorite to play because the archers and bats can very easily hit you without you even noticing. 

- [b] A bit buggy: [/b] The game is plagued with small, but annoying bugs. Some people apparently get softlocked on tiers of upgrading, or stuck in a room. There is a particularly annoying bug where the game resets your flooring to the first state you ever put down.

- [b]Misc:[/b] Snail Form is too hard to obtain, and is the only unlock I have left to find. I've run so many full runs and haven't gotten a single snail drop. I'd recommend allowing the fish merchant to sell the object, or alternatively, making them a guaranteed spawn in a certain room.


[h1]Overall:[/h1]

Cult of the Lamb's visual style is flawless. The gameplay is very fun, and the writing is well crafted and enjoyable. It is a good time well worth every cent I paid for, with a solid ending that tied everything together nicely. If you're looking for a cute, endearing game that will make you laugh and challenge you, please, buy this game!

That all being said: 

Cult of the Lamb it is not a flawless experience. It falls short of becoming the absolute best version of itself. It can learn so much from games in its genre - Enter the Gungeon's diverse selection of upgrades and weapons, Binding of Isaac's meaningful unlocks and gameplay modes, etc.

Not every game has to be this way, of course. Cult of the Lamb could exist as it is now and it would still be, at least, a great time. But it's capable of so much more, and I genuinely hope this company commits to nurturing it. I could easily see 20 hours becoming 200+ with the right work being done on it.

Okay, so I went into Cult of the Lamb expecting some cute, mindless dungeon crawling.  What I got was a surprisingly deep and emotionally engaging experience. Yes, it's adorable – the art style is fantastic, the little lamb protagonist is charming, and the followers are undeniably cute.  The dungeon crawling is fun, challenging enough to be engaging without being frustrating.  I actually really enjoyed the combat; it's simple but effective, and finding new weapons and abilities kept me coming back for more.
 
But the real hook? The cult management.  I'm not gonna lie, I got way too attached to my followers.  I named them all, I built them the best houses, I made sure they were always fed and happy.  And then...I sacrificed some of them to eldritch gods.  It was necessary for the greater good of the cult, of course, but it still felt...bad.  The game cleverly plays on that emotional tug-of-war, making you care about your followers even as you're making difficult choices that affect their fate.
 
The strategic element of managing resources, keeping morale high, and balancing the needs of your cult with the demands of dungeon crawling was surprisingly intricate and rewarding.  I found myself constantly tweaking my strategies, trying to optimize everything for maximum cult growth and happiness.  It's a surprisingly addictive loop.
 
While the repetitive nature of the dungeon runs might bore some players after a while, the constant upgrades and the ever-evolving needs of my cult kept me hooked.  Overall, Cult of the Lamb exceeded my expectations.  It's a unique blend of cute and creepy, strategic and emotional.  Highly recommended, but be prepared for some unexpected feelings along the way.

[h1]A cute little funny dungeon crawler, with cute little animals.[/h1]

Do you ever wanted to make your own Cult? Set up your own rules and decide how to tread your minions? Don't look further! This game comes with a free power fantasy!

Also don't get distracted by the artstyle. This game gets really dark very fast!


[h1]Story:[/h1]

Usually I would now say that I won't spoil anything, but there is not much to spoil. You are a Lamb... A sacrifice made for the old gods! But in the afterlife... In the far distance you can hear the howl of an even older god! Pledge loyalty to your new lord and avenge your death. Kill your tormentors! Create your own Cult! Build up your settlement!

But be careful not make your new "friend" angry! You don't want to be sacrificed again... Do you?


[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]

[b]The gameplay is split up in multiple parts![/b]


[b]Build up your Settlement:[/b]
Having a Cult is a lot of business. You have to take care of your little friends and keep them busy with work or by praising you! Even feeding them is your job... and cleaning up. In fact they would propably die without you, but in exchange you will get EXP points and other rewards. They even give you ressources and more!

In the end it is like that: Make your followers happy = Profit!

The happier they are the more EXP they will drop when you sacrifice them. Oh... Yes you can also sacrifice them. If you really don't like someone, just kill them on the next midnight mass. The other followers are going to love it, because you are always in the right!

There are even more activities to do, but that would take away all the fun!

The base building is also a lot of fun! Next to useful buildings like tents or woodcutter shacks, you can also decorate your village. 


[b]Fighting:[/b]
Fight your way through dungeons, unlock new abilities and gather materials for your little village! Some things are also locked behind some levels you need to pass first. There are all in all 5 dungeons, made out of multiple segements. Each run is different and the drops are always randomized! You can get better gear or better drops the more you progress and by leveling up specific skills! It feels like your average rouge-lite!

Next to bossfights you will also have the ability to rescue and hire new cult members and enter an "infinite dungeon" with even more rewards!

Dying is also not really a problem. You will just lose a bit of your loot and thats it. It is pretty fair. This is what I liked about the whole gameplay mechanic. I am not really a fan of games like "The Binding of Isaac", because they are just too brutal. But "Cult of the Lamb" finds the right mix between random events, hard encounters and fun, while being far less punishing!

The combat is fairly easy! You have your dodgerole and your attack. Thats it. You also have a special power! Your weapons and powers are always randomized and always different at each new start!


[h1]Atmosphere:[/h1]

Really good! The world is very interesting and it makes a lot of fun to explore. You will meet a lot of NPCs, with interesting stories to tell. There are also minigames like fishing and more! Outside of the dungeons, it is a pretty relaxed gameplay. If you don't want to fight you don't have to either. You can spend a few days just chilling in your village or explore the surroundings! The whole world is just feels so alive and colorful!


[h1]Music:[/h1]

Exactly what you would expect from such a game:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nf-CUmxX3GY


[h1]Graphics:[/h1]

I am not a fan of jokes in reviews, but this game gave me diabetes just by being so sweet. It just looks so clean and cute! I love this kind of artstyle.


[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]

If you like "The Binding of Isaac" or "Don't Starve", this game is worth a look! Even if you are not a fan of these games you might want to give this one a try! You can feel the love the developers put into this game and on top of that it has the typical "Devolver Digital" quality!

A nice, cute and short video game. Also, don't get confused by the "roguelike" tags, this actually shouldn't be considered one and I've no idea why people think it is.

Why? When you say "roguelike" people immediately imagine a video game with a really long progression system, a lot of replayability, with a ton of content and playable for dozens of hours, usually even more than a hundred before you actually do everything there is to do. This game simply doesn't have that. It's a relatively short but sweet mix of light dungeon crawling and light colony management. You can probably beat it in 10 hours if you play it on a normal difficulty and don't try to go for all the side content. And once you finish the game, that's pretty much it, there's very little reason to come back top it and play it past that point.

So, if you're looking for a roguelike, this isn't it. Don't get confused by the tags. So if that's what you're looking for, you should turn back and walk away. But if you want to play a really enjoyable little game for a couple of evenings, then this is definitely it!

[h2]Introduction[/h2]

Cult of the Lamb is greater than the sum of its parts. It doesn't quite achieve rogue-like or base-building legendary status, but the overall package is elevated higher than its reach.

[h2]Story[/h2]

You're a lamb sacrificed by four gods named "the bishops of old faith." Upon death, you meet an imprisoned fifth bishop named "The One Who Waits." The One Who Waits provides a crown embued with godly powers, tasks you to start a cult in his name, and kill the other four bishops.

The story is a simple one, but I never felt I wanted more. It's a solid foundation for satirical humor, and the religious references are funny and land often.

As things progress the game rewards you with little tidbits about your origin and place among the bishops. It's all light fare and works well.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

I didn't know I needed a genre blend of rogue-like, bullet-hell combat combined with the progression of a base-builder, but it's a beautiful balance.

Combining these genres creates a nice pace where you do a dungeon run to collect resources and hurry home to take care of your followers. The flow is reinforced by a daily timer prominently displayed at all times. I also appreciated how your cult's base progression advances combat strength. Outside of combat and base building is a variety of minigames, including fishing, a gambling dice-based game, and other cults to visit and exploit.

[h2]Base Building and Your Cult[/h2]

The gameplay is fun and addicting but never very deep.

There are familiar elements like resource gathering to build new structures and you can refine resources to create more advanced structures.

You need to farm to feed your growing cult and use their feces to fertilize new crops. If followers get hungry or unhappy for any reason, they will dissent and start spreading ant-gospel to everyone else. You can then imprison them until they learn to behave or sacrifice them for meat to feed followers.

Followers level up, and you can send them on adventures to get resources or bring back new people to indoctrinate.

There is the ability to customize every follower's appearance and there are endless unlockable decorations to personalize your base.

The base-building gameplay loop is tied to the cycle of a new day. Each day resets cooldowns like sermons and rituals. Both sermons and rituals boost cult morale. However, rituals have special effects like making everyone feel full for a couple of days, motivated to work tirelessly through the night, or building extra devotion by marrying a follower (wed multiple if you want but they'll get jealous when they witness you smooch another.) You can then extract devotion to level up combat abilities or unlock new structures.

Base progression is well done, and I liked how advanced structures automated farming and other mundane tasks. I was growing bored of some repetitive tasks right around the time I unlocked structures that let my cult do it for me. Nothing is overly complex or overstays it's welcome.

[h2]Adventuring and Killing in the Name of Your God[/h2]

As with base-building, the combat part is also pretty simple. There is a spammable weapon attack, a dodge-roll, a resource-based magic ability, and a charge attack that uses the same magic resource but at a slower rate.

There are several weapon types, such as daggers, swords, axes, and heavy hammers. The only change in gameplay from weapons is attack speed, damage, and how long you're left open after an attack. 

Weapons can also have a single modifier type. There is nothing too crazy here with the usual assortment of poison, crits, health-leeching, or the chance to spawn a little ghost that will attack a nearby enemy. All the modifiers play the same and only add more random damage that the player doesn't control. The crit weapons always give the most bonus and make other options feel trivial.

Enemies range in size, speed, and attack patterns. They flash a moment before they attack. You can dodge-roll at any time and even when charging up your own attack. Other enemies spew projectiles on the screen in bullet-hell fashion.

Your first priority is to avoid damage. Watch for the spew of bullets and enemy charge attacks. Next, get in as much damage as you can. Each weapon has a combo string, with the final hit doing a nice bit of extra damage. The slower the weapon, the shorter the string. There are also charge attacks, but I never found them to be an efficient use of your magic resource.
There are a bunch of magic cooldowns with various ranges and functionality like AOE pushbacks, long-range seeking missiles, and temporary invincibility. The resource requirement is well-tuned, and abilities feel powerful but not overpowered.

The combat loop is fast and fun, if rarely challenging for the seasoned player of these genres. 

[h2]Graphics[/h2]

Cult of the Lamb lives on its presentation and deservedly so. You can't go wrong with cute animals and satanic overtones. Every sprite is lovingly crafted and often hilarious. The animations are excellent, too. I never grew tired of watching Lambert open his cult bible, hover in the air, and extract every bit of devotion from his followers.

There is a large cast of characters and places to see other than your own base and the procedural dungeons. One favorite was a town where the cult leader was obsessed with gold and all things shiny. All his followers were dipped in melted gold and could only shake to acknowledge his presence.

[h2]Sound[/h2]

The music is catchy and memorable. I liked the sound effects, too. With any base-building game, you're bound to hear the same blips and beeps over and over. The effects were always crispy and satisfying. There is no voice acting, but the animalese-like chatter is themed to each character. The spider has a SssSss to his voice, and the fish has an underwater blooping to his tone. The voices always made me laugh.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

Cult of the Lamb is a smart game with tons of features and ideas going for it. That said, it plays things safe. The base building is approachable but too simple and one step away from greatness. The combat is good but never as exhilarating as some of its rogue-like peers. However, the presentation and humor are excellent and make Cult of the Lamb feel special enough not to be missed.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
[list]
[*]Genuinely funny
[*]Great pacing and blending of genres
[*]Fun, addicting, and doesn't overstay its welcome
[/list]
[h2]Cons[/h2]
[list]
[*]Combat would benefit from more variety
[*]Base-building remains essentially the same from hour one to hour twenty
[/list]

[h2]Challenge[/h2]

I played the game on "Very Hard." There are several levels of difficulty that adjust how much health you have, how much damage you take, and how quickly your followers get hungry or sick. I found the game relatively easy and desired a bit more challenge. The final encounters were fantastic and a great example of what's possible within the game's framework; I just wish there was more of it.

Cult of the Lamb truly has become a cult favorite for many obvious reasons. While the game has been overhyped it doesn't fall short of major expectations (given there are some flaws which I will address). Cult of the Lamb combines many aspects of some of my favorite games that I adored which made it highly enjoyable (Garden Story, Turnip Boy Escapes Tax Evasion, Needy Streamer Overload). Without a doubt, I would recommend this game 1000%.

Weeks leading up to the launch of the game, all I would hear was the excitement and hype for Cult of the Lamb literally everywhere. At the time, I wasn't sure if it was something I would enjoy as I've never played a roguelike game before, yet alone understood what the tag meant. Based on the art alone, I knew it would be something I'd like because it was so cute, but art can often be very deceiving and misleading. I deliberated for a week until I tried the demo and instantly fell in love with the game and bought it right away despite the price tag.

The overall concept of this game is both creative and humorous. You've been resurrected and given a second chance at life, but as a cult leader who brainwashes, embezzles, extorts, and feeds your followers poop. There are four bishops (bosses) you need to fight before the last boss, and in order to encounter each of the bishops, you need to do each dungeon a minimum of four times. Dungeons are nicely designed; the 2.5D environment fits the game so well. I really can't imagine the game in 2D or 3D; it just wouldn't feel right. The cult base, dungeon environment, and followers aesthetic is cute, but also mildly creepy at the same time, which really is appropriate for the overarching theme of the game.

The micromanaging/colony sim part of the game was probably where I spent most of my time. It can definitely feel like a chore for those who aren't into it, but it was rather enjoyable for me. There are tons of options when it comes to customizing your followers and decorating your base. I like being able to move things around to my liking, but it felt super buggy at times and I hope the devs patch it soon. Sometimes the hammer won't go where you want it to go and certain tiles are really hard to move around. The customization and freedom also expanded into how you want to run your cult, such as your doctrines and rituals, which was a nice touch, meaning no two cults are the same.

While I really do enjoy the game and can without a doubt say its made it onto my list of favorite games I've played this year, there are a few things about Cult of the Lamb that feel unpolished or a bit lackluster. You definitely don't play the game for story, so don't expect anything in that department. The music soundtrack is okay - nothing too special or memorable. After the first two bosses/dungeons, things really start to feel repetitive; no additional special mechanics were introduced to keep the game fresh. If mechanics did get introduced – all you had to do was dodge just like before. I also felt that some weapons and curses/fervor abilities were super chunky and clunky to use. Another issue that I hope devs will address is the lag with the cult base after having a certain amount of followers (I know the issue is not due to my pc specs).

Overall, the game is still enjoyable, and fulfilling but could be so much more. I wish there was more content for how much it cost. The dungeon runs and boss fights are rather short and if you do the bare minimum for the cult simulator and management of the game - gameplay is probably like 5-7 hours max, which is insanely short. The other aspects of the game such as the knucklebones (dice game) and fishing are whatever - I wouldn't really consider it content unless you’re achievement hunting. I would not call the game a masterpiece, but still a great and enjoyable game with some flaws. The interactions with followers probably is the best thing in the game and has made me laugh on multiple occasions.

The devs did a great job of adding their own spin to these while also including base building and follower management. It’s really got a little bit of a lot of genres. There’s even some lite bullet hell sequences based on enemy and boss abilities. And there are some mini games as well. :)

The story is pretty silly. A group of monster bishops go about the business of sacrificing all lambs in the world. You’re the last lamb, but when they sacrifice you, an evil god intervenes, making you his avatar in the world. Your goal is to found and build up a cult to his worship while building up your cult’s base to feed and shelter your cultists, gather their worship energy, and generally build both your power and the power of your cultists. You will use your cult’s base as the launching point for various quests including your other primary goal: to kill the bishops that have imprisoned your god.

The base building is not disimilar from various RTS games. You’ll build a variety of buildings that will accomodate your religion and your cultists. You’ll also farm, mine, cut lumber, cook food, gather that worship energy I mentioned earlier. You’ll (unfortunately) also clean up your cultist’s poop, which they’ll drop indiscriminately around your base until you finally build some outhouses, and even then, they’ll let it go sometimes. Freaking animals! You’ll also also build a prison to discourage dissent amongst your followers, crypts for the dead, etc..

Your cultists can and will die despite never leaving your compound outside of some story moments when they’re summoned elsewhere. Some will grow old and die of old age. You’ll sacrifice others. Depending on circumstances, cultists can also murder each other. However, they also develop relationships amongst themselves and with you, and maintaining your relationship with your cultists is of paramount importance.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3136751070

Then there are the dungeons. These are presented in Binding of Isaac fashion. However, this isn’t a twin stick shooter. Instead, it’s melee and magic focused, where you’ll use weapons, relics, and sometimes actual spells to fight your way through each dungeon. However, it strays from Isaac by also including node maps between dungeons that might also include new followers, supplies, extra battles, etc…The Zelda mechanics show themselves in the actual combat. Plus, there is a heart health system which is used in both of CotL’s main influences.

The node system will eventually lead to the area boss, who you will defeat and then recruit. In each bishop’s area, you’ll need to complete them four times. The fourth time, it unlocks the bishop battle.

The world also features other locations where you’ll meet allies and complete quests and such. Which leads me to the RPG mechanics. You will have several categories of unlocks, from weapons and relics to rituals (which you’ll use for buffs, resurrecting dead cultists, and so on), new buildings and decorations, etc…there are a lot of upgrades and many tiers to some of them.

So yeah. There’s a lot to Cult of the Lamb, and I’m really just scratching the surface of what is available in the game. Once you finish the game, you can keep playing, wrapping up cheevos and doing some extra story stuff if you’re so inclined. You also unlock some difficulty modes.

The graphics and audio are all geared towards emphasizing the cutesy and yet murdery nature of the world. It’s a very pleasing game mixed with pleasing horror, lol. And the soundtrack was really cool as well.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3136751294

I will also note that despite the various gameplay mechanics, the game does a great job of teaching you how to play in a very approachable and intuitive manner.

It took me right around 13 hours to play through the campaign, but I think you could easily get another 10ish hours trying to wrap up cheevos. I played on the Steam Deck on the highest settings with no issues and about 2 hour battery life.

Cost vs value is definitely there with this one. The devs do recommend using a gamepad, so if you’re strictly k/m, you might want to look more into it before buying, but it’s an easy recommendation and one of the best Indies out there.

Cult of the Lamb is a game with so much potential that I ended up disappointed in it only being 'good' when the experience could have been 'extraordinary'. It's a game worth playing that I'd recommend for rogue-lite fans, but it's not a must-play. It is very flashy and polished in aesthetic, but lacks substance.

This conclusion surprised me. 

In my first ~5ish hours of gameplay, the UX design,  character movement, art style, music, and core gameplay loop felt too good to be true. This first impression instilled in me an enthusiastic optimism for a high quality experience, but I was left wanting for the remainder of my play-through. 

The gameplay loop felt repetitive and arduous sooner than I'd hoped. The roguelite aspect and combat system felt like an afterthought with unclear hit detection, deprived of depth or variety. The game is too easy until you hit a disproportionate difficulty spike late-game. 

The colony management aspect grew burdensome, and the in-game economy didn't feel balanced. By the time I unlocked everything and built my colony, I realized how inconsequential the tech-tree is and regretted the extra time and effort it all took. I experienced frequent run-ending frame drops, and bugs ranging from disappearing followers, to the inability to interact with my buildings without rebooting the game. 

Despite all of this though, I still had my fair share of fun and don't regret the purchase. There is a lot to like about it. The UI, Score, and overall aesthetic are brilliant. The controls feel snappy and responsive. The game consistently delivers humor and charm.  I noticed how much potential exists in the roguelite-colony concept, and am impressed with the amount of effort spent on unexpected, minute details. I just wish these efforts were reallocated to the parts of the gameplay that really mattered. This *could have been* a masterpiece.

Cult of the Lamb it made me smile enough to prevent me from leaving a negative review, and I'm a sucker for good art and music direction. It's not a great roguelite, nor is it a great colony-sim. It's 'good enough' if you want something to kill time, and are attracted to the aesthetic.

I recommend this game. However, be aware that there's not much content here, and it grows repetitive rather quickly. It's a trend that I've seen happening with some similar games like Moonlighter, where the developers try to include a bunch of different elements just for all of them to end up feeling rather simple and underdeveloped.

Let's start with the "roguelite" component. You can play through 4 different dungeons in the style of a roguelite. Go to a proceduraly generated dungeon, get resources, grow stronger, repeat. However, while in games like Dead Cells or TBOI you can do this for hundreds (if not thousands) of hours and still find it entertaining due to the plethora of different options at your disposal, in Cult of the Lamb you only have a handful of weapons and skills, and they are not that different from each other. Each run feels exactly the same, so they end up growing quite boring once you've done a couple of them. There's no reason to keep doing dungeons once you've unlocked everything.

Then you have the "management" component. Manage your cult, control your cultists and build your temple. Again, this falls into the same fate. There's not enough depth here as to sink many hours into it. The game doesn't give you too many options, so after a while you run out of things to do.

Those are the two core elements of the gameplay, and as I've said, neither is deep enough to provide much entertainment. Aside from that, it's artystic style is really good, it has cool designs, it's soundtrack is nice and it's story is ok for what it is (little more than a couple of dialogues). Don't buy this game if you are looking for a roguelite with hundreds of hours of content. Don't buy it if you are expecting a management game in the vein of Stardew Valley. Buy this game if you want a cute game that will be fun for a dozen of hours or so. Tbh, I would just wait until it's on sale, $23 feels a little bit too expensive for what you got.

I’m a straight-A physics student who thought nothing could shake my dedication to science. Then I stumbled upon Cult of the Lamb, and everything changed. I spent the last 20 days so deep in this game that I forgot what a textbook looks like. Somehow, I still managed to ace my exams. Turns out, leading a cult of adorable critters is great training for managing a hectic academic life.

I started with the intention of playing just a little here and there. Yeah, right. This game grabbed hold of me and didn’t let go. I unlocked all the achievements in 20 days. TWENTY. DAYS. That’s 480 hours that could’ve gone into studying the mysteries of the universe, but instead, I was brainwashing fluffy animals and performing bizarre rituals. Why so easy, you ask? It wasn’t. It was pure, unfiltered obsession.

The gameplay? Ridiculously addictive. Running a cult of cute followers, making them worship me, and performing dark rituals was surprisingly therapeutic. My physics books collected dust while I perfected my digital cult leadership skills. Even Einstein would be impressed with my newfound commitment.

The art style? Dangerously cute. It lures you in with charming visuals, but underneath lies a game so compelling you’ll sacrifice real-life responsibilities to keep playing. “Just one more ritual,” I’d tell myself, while my physics notes sat neglected. My professors might wonder about my time management, but at least my cult was thriving.

Achievement hunting? A walk in the park, not because the game is easy, but because I was driven by an unholy urge to unlock everything. If only I could harness this level of determination in my studies, I’d probably be on my way to winning a Nobel Prize.

In conclusion, Cult of the Lamb is a dangerously addictive game that will make you rethink your life choices. If you’re a student, take this as a warning: your GPA might wobble, but your cult will flourish. Five stars. Would sacrifice my studies for fluffy followers again.

This game is very fun. I like the base management, and managing your followers, etc etc, there are some clear "good" and "bad" weapons imo, and which weapon you get is random, but otherwise, the combat section of this game is fun too, but this game is also very frustrating. It is a bit buggy, descriptions of buildings / upgrades / mechanics are vague, or are just never explained, and then the game punishes you for not understanding these mechanics.

overall I'll give it a positive review, but i think I'd only give it like a 6.5/10, because I had a lot of fun playing the game and because while bugs weren't particularly rare, they weren't exactly common either, but this game could easily be an 8, without the all problems mentioned above, and below. despite the fact this is a positive review, I'm going to go over the bugs I encountered, and the "bad" mechanics, because those are the things i want to talk about, and talking about both the good and bad parts of the game would make this review too long.

Your followers can give you quests to do, which give you loyalty (XP for an individual follower) and Faith (general "happiness" of your followers), these quests are timed, and if you do not complete them in time you lose 40 faith (50%) with your followers. normally this isn't a problem, as these quests are fairly easy to complete, and they give the quest giver a lot of xp, so they will probably level up, which gives you devotion (xp for you) immediately, and increases the amount of devotion they generate at your shrine, which allows you to buy new buildings, or buy upgrades for existing buildings, so when you see a quest you'll want to complete it, but there is a bug with quests where sometimes they will simply fail immediately after you pick them up. causing you to lose a TON of faith, and the only way to prevent this is to simply never do quests (which also makes you lose faith, but less of it).  I've found reddit threads, and steam discussions dating up to 3 years back reporting this bug, and some of them even got dev replies, but I encountered this bug twice just in my first session playing the game, so it can clearly still happen, and it happened super early game for me, which caused some problems.

you see, when your faith gets too low, your followers can begin dissenting against you. dissenting followers do not work, reduce your faith, and can make other followers dissent against you, who will of course also not work, and reduce your faith even more. how do you deal with dissenting followers? well it's simple. you put them in jail and re-educate them, or just kill them. but you need to unlock the prison, and I didn't have the prison unlocked, and sacrificing followers causes you to lose EVEN MORE faith, unless you unlock a certain perk, that I didn't take (and I didn't want to sacrifice my followers anyways).

there were a couple other minor bugs that occurred during my playthrough, but the only other one worth mentioning is that followers can sometimes just disappear. not die, not leave, disappear. I sent a follower on a mission to retrieve some resources and he returned with a debuff, but alive, gave me the resources I sent him to collect, and I then went on a crusade (dungeon) and he was gone. he was not anywhere in my base, and he could not be resurrected. this wouldn't be so bad, but the follower happened to be Yarlen, who is a unique follower from from the Pilgrim Pack dlc, which costs irl money. Yarlen is functionally identical to any other follower with the exception of his name, and that he gives you quests unique to him. I've already done his quests, so it's not the end of the world, but he had a Gold Skull Necklace he took with him which sucks, and again, I paid money for that dlc, I don't think it's unreasonable to be upset that part of the dlc was inexplicably missing.

I did manage to find a solution to this bug, and got my follower back. apparently changing languages and then changing it back will make your follower reappear (of all things...), so maybe I'm just nit-picky, but it had me worried for a while because, I have other unique followers, including one who can't age, and one who can't starve who I'd like to keep.

moving out of bug territory, while progressing through the game, I unlocked the ritual of resurrection, which, as the name implies, allows me to revive a follower for 75 bones (ritual resource). I specifically picked this ritual over another, because I thought being able to revive followers would be great, but the game fails to mention that this ritual has a downside, where revived followers have a chance to come back with the Catatonic trait, or the Cursed trait.

the Catatonic trait makes followers hide in the corners of the map, and wander aimlessly around the base not doing anything, while the Cursed trait does the same, with the added effect that a follower with this trait is a zombie that can kill other followers.

I, of course, got cursed on my first revive.

so, how do you fix this? well in order to heal it you'll need 20 flowers 20 mushrooms, and 20 Crystal Shards, which is simple enough if you actually know where they come from. but the game doesn't tell you, and by the time I had unlocked the resurrection, i was only just about to enter my 2nd (of 4) zones- the one which gives mushrooms. so I had a zombie running around my base, with only the flowers required to heal him, I had only JUST found where to get mushrooms, and had no idea where to get the crystal shards. at this point I had unlocked prisons, but only had 1, which was being taken up by my dissenter from above, so my options were to spend bones I no longer had to sacrifice the zombie, heal the zombie with resources I did not have, or know where to get, or make a new prison, with wood I also did not have, because I JUST used it to make a currently occupied prison.

by the time I got the resources needed to imprison him, he had killed one of my followers, and when i finally had all the resources I needed to heal him, the zombie was elderly, which meant even if I cured him, he would not work, and would die of age in the next few days anyways.

mid-way through the game, you'll unlock a new resource you can get from your followers called Sin. you generate sin through a variety of methods, but the important part is that you fill up a bar on a follower, collect their sin, and the bar resets to 0. sometimes when collecting their sin, followers can become "damned". a damned follower is teleported away, and will ambush you on your next crusade. becoming a re-occurring enemy and after beating them enough times you get an extra sin, and they can be re-indoctrinated into your cult. 

but the game doesn't ever tell you HOW your followers become damned. according to the wiki this happens after a you take a sin from a follower 3 times in a row, but this doesn't seem to be 100% accurate, as I've harvested 2 sin from follower A, harvested 1 from follower B and then go back to follower A and they still get damned, and I've damned followers, got them back, and got a sin from them without damning them after ignoring them for a while, so it's not 3 total either. your followers have randomly generated traits, including some which increase (or decrease) sin generation, so naturally if you get a follower that increases sin generation, you'll want to use that follower to generate sin, but if you try, you'll end up with a damned follower. the extra sin you gain from beating the damned follower is nice, but I can get more faster by staying in my base, so it feels like I'm being punished by a vague mechanic the game doesn't even tell you exists, which feels bad imo.

🌟 [b][i]Visually Stunning, Darkly Charming[/i][/b] 🌟

Cult of The Lamb is an absolute visual delight with its unique art style that’s both adorable and creepy in the best ways. The aesthetic really pulls you in, setting it apart from the sea of other games in the genre.

💖 [b]What I Loved[/b]

- [b]Visuals[/b]: The art style is a huge draw. It’s rare to find a game that can be cute, eerie, and brutal all at once, and Cult of The Lamb nails it.
- [b]Fun Mechanics[/b]: From bizarre rituals and the sheer novelty of interacting with things like poop, to conducting sacrifices, there’s always something unexpected around the corner.
- [b]Addictive Base-Building[/b]: Building and managing a cult compound is surprisingly addictive. The progression keeps you coming back as you improve your base and grow your followers.

👎 [b]Where It Falls Short[/b]

- [b]Repetitive Gameplay Loop[/b]: While entertaining at first, the core gameplay loop can feel repetitive pretty quickly. Once you’ve got the hang of it, there’s not much variation in what you’re doing day-to-day.
- [b]Rogue-Like Combat is Just “Meh”[/b]: The action segments try to capture the dynamic, snappy combat style of games like Hades, but it doesn’t quite get there. It feels a bit clunky and could use some fine-tuning to be as engaging.
- [b]Performance Hiccups[/b]: Surprisingly CPU-heavy. On a high-end setup (Ryzen 5950x), I still saw occasional frame drops down to 80 FPS when my base was more built up, which seemed unnecessary.

🎯 [b]Overall Verdict[/b]

Cult of The Lamb is a memorable experience with a truly distinct artistic vision, and while it has its downsides, I’ve been having a great time. If it’s become so popular, it’s mostly thanks to its stunning art and quirky charm.

This is a tough one.

i REALLY want to be able to recommend this game, because for the first few hours it felt like one of the best indie roguelikes I've played, with an amazing theme and cute artstyle. Combat feels enjoyable and the fusion of a cult management sim is a wonderful combination.

Unfortunately once you pass those first few hours you begin to realise how truly shallow most of the systems are. Doctrines and individual skill trees are literally thrown at you early on, which results in a massive influx of new toys to play with and progression, and then everything just grinds to halt after a few hours once you get the grip of everything. To the point where the only 'choice' in the game will be choosing between two doctrines - and some are just outright better than others to the point where they just completely break the game (Looking at you, Grass Eater and Ritual of Enrichment) which results in you either throwing balance out the window or deciding to intentionally gimp yourself. Every choice comes down between two options and that's it, most outcomes being completely useless anyway. 

Your cult skill trees means nothing when it is literally inevitable that you cap out and unlock everything likely before beating the final boss - which begs the question, what's the point? Why would you ever play the game more than once when there will likely be zero difference between your first cult and your second. 
It's the equivalent of Borderlands having the level cap be 100 and just allowing you to eventually take every point on each Vault Hunters skill try - why would you want that?

That spells the main problem with the game. There is zero opportunity cost in any of your decisions. Zero variety of any 'builds'  for your cult, followers, or combat style across the whole game. Followers are disposable since there's always more of them, the individual 'traits' they each get are laughable at best, the amount of days that pass mean absolutely nothing (it would be cool if enemies got tougher the longer time went on, in order to force you to budget your time and weigh risks etc, ala XCOM), weapon and curse variety is god-awful. And if you make the claim that combat is only a 'small' part of a game that's meant to be a cult management sim, then I ask: why are both parts of the game just as shallow as each other?

All bosses, and minibosses, save for perhaps the boss of the third area, are ridiculously easy (including the final boss sadly) 

This unfortunately means once you've beaten the game...that's it. You've...beaten the game. And a second playthrough would be just that - doing everything a second time, the exact same way. No post-game, no new game+, nothing.

My theory is this game will quickly go from 'Very positive' - as it is now - to either Mostly, or even mixed, as time goes on and more people begin to finish the game and realise there's nothing more to it.

That doesn't even mention the bugs. For a title like this, the amount of game-breaking bugs this game somehow has is insane, insta-fail quests, invisible and invulnerable summoned enemies bricking my crusades, constant micro-stuttering in dungeons, enemies in cocoons that refuse to come out for 5+ minutes and more - are all things I experienced in my short time with the game, and other people have had far worse things including several ways of getting softlocked and completely bricking your save.

That's of course not to say the game is terrible - it's absolutely not. I had my fun with it, and the soundtrack, visuals, and dialogue were all very good. But after finishing the game in just 17 hours, that means that for the price I paid (£19.49), that equals out to less than an hour of playtime per £1 spent - does that seem worth it to you? Think of the amount of hours you can squeeze out of Issac, or Hades.

I feel like this game needs a big overhaul to justify its price tag, and perhaps some DLC for post-game content. Which I really believe can be done, this game has a brilliant base to build on, but there's just no meat on the bones yet, for lack of a better term. I really do hope I can come back in the future and change this review to a positive one, but for right now I just can't recommend this.

Cult of the Lamb has a lot of promise but fails to deliver on a couple fronts. Here's what I liked:
 - the soundtrack is excellent
 - the art style is fun and cute
 - the idea is good at its core
 - managing my cult was addictive and kept me up past my bedtime

Unfortunately, that's not enough to carry the game. Cult of the Lamb suffers from serious shallowness. The combat is really poorly executed -- targeting and frames feel unreliable. There's also no depth to combat. You are given a random weapon and a random right click cast ability each dungeon run. The only difference between the weapons is their attack rate/animation and damage. You can upgrade weapon damage and special effects as a whole from your cult base, but it doesn't add depth, just numbers. The same is largely true for the curses. Combat movement is all just rolling and attacking, no special moves or attack combos. 

Enemy mobs aren't very unique. They wind up and slash, spit orbs, jump and land, the usual stuff. I'm about 3/4 of the way through the game and haven't found a particularly innovative or unique boss or mob yet. Every dungeon run feels basically the same, it just lacks any real complexity. 

As for managing your cult, it's extremely fun at first, but soon becomes a slog. Once you have 10+ cult members you're not going to want to go around blessing each one for faith improvements. It soon becomes apparent that base upgrades aren't actually game-changing or interesting. In fact, many of them just automate tasks that you shouldn't have to do from the start. 

For example, your cultists can chop wood and mine stone and plant seeds, but they can't harvest crops or clean up their own shit unless you build the right t3 building for it. Yes, you need a t3 building just to eliminate the slog of harvesting crops. 

The other decisions you can make at your cult base are equally bland. Changing your cult doctrines isn't as interesting as it could be -- the doctrines are usually negligible or have one choice that's clearly better than the other. Honestly most of the doctrines haven't changed my game at all. So my followers get a faith bonus when I upgrade their homes -- completely meaningless since their faith is maxed out most of the time anyway from just doing basic upkeep and care. 

There's no real sense of choice or strategy when building your cult. You can unlock all upgrades, and you will -- quickly. I was almost finished with all the tech trees halfway through the game. You don't really build your cult per se -- it feels pretty on rails. Sure you can choose where you put buildings, but there's not much else by way of agency. 

Also, the game is stuffed to the gills with decoration bloat. You're supposed to be jazzed to unlock new blueprints but they're all just meaningless decorations that you're not gonna waste much time on anyway. You don't need them, they grant no bonuses, and they just clutter up the base. I would be more interested in customizing and building out an aesthetically pleasing base if I had any real agency over my cult.

All told, this game is shallow as it is now. I would recommend buying it at $15 if it goes on sale to that price level. Right now $25 is too steep -- the game just hasn't delivered on its idea in-depth. The game could benefit from the devs revisiting combat to make it more complex and challenging, or to give it some additional strategic depth and uniqueness between crusades. As for the cult management, certain processes should probably be automated from the start. It would also be nice to see more actual choice in terms of the direction your cult goes in, and the impacts that has on your playstyle. As it stands now, impacts from cult choices are minimal to nonexistent. 

All told, I'd give the game a 6/10 right now. The first several hours are addictive as hell, but you'll soon find yourself getting bored and a little sick of picking crops and cleaning up shit.

[h1]Cult of the Lamb: 100% Achievement Completion Review[/h1]

- [b]Adorable Yet Sinister Vibes[/b]: Who knew running a cult could be this cute? You start off as a tiny lamb with an adorable face, but soon, you're turning unsuspecting woodland creatures into loyal followers. It's [i]precious[/i]... until you make them sacrifice each other.

- [b]Playtime[/b]: If you're in for the long haul, expect around 40–50 hours to complete all achievements (depending on how much you like to optimize and grind). It's a satisfying mix of combat, resource management, and, of course, heretic slaughter.

- [b]Cult Management 101[/b]: You’re not just slaying enemies—you're managing your cult like a CEO. From building shrines to convincing your followers to worship you, it’s all about [i]cultivation[/i] (pun intended). Be prepared to spend hours making sure no one gets too angry, or else... well, it’s ritual sacrifice time.

- [b]Combat is Addictive[/b]: The dungeon crawling is fast-paced, with an almost "one-more-run" mentality. With every upgrade, you feel more powerful, and the bosses? They’ll make you sweat a little. Or a lot.

[h2]Achievements Breakdown[/h2]
- [b]All Followers Saved[/b]: Good luck getting them to stay loyal. It's a game of psychological manipulation and pestering them for gifts. But when they all love you? It's pure cult leader satisfaction.
- [b]Building Master[/b]: Building shrines, farms, and decorations—nothing says "successful cult" like an entirely decorated shrine and a veggie farm in the back.
- [b]All Bosses Defeated[/b]: Every boss fight is a unique challenge. By the end of it, you’re the god of destruction [i]and[/i] the best worship leader around.

- [b]Visuals & Soundtrack[/b]: This game is a visual masterpiece with an adorably dark twist. The environments are quirky and fun, with a seriously catchy soundtrack that’ll have you humming "Cult of the Lamb" long after you’ve put the game down.

- [b]Difficulty[/b]: It’s a challenge, but nothing too overwhelming. You'll find yourself powering through tough dungeons and then collecting those hard-to-get resources with ease. Achieving everything feels like a well-earned reward!

- [b]Replayability[/b]: Even after completing all the achievements, the game has that "just one more run" charm. You can always build a new cult or experiment with different builds to see how far you can push the game’s systems.

[h2]Final Recommendation[/h2]
- 10/10 would recommend. Whether you’re a fan of roguelikes, managing quirky systems, or just like watching a cult of adorable animals grow in power, [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] offers a wickedly fun experience. I can't think of a better game to invest hours into, and I guarantee you’ll get hooked. Just don’t forget to feed your followers... and maybe sacrifice a few when they start questioning your divine power.

The kind of game that needs an "indifferent" rating to me - it's... good? Would I go and tell anyone "you've gotta go play Cult of the Lamb"? Nah. Would I tell anyone not to bother? Nah. It's a solid game. 

Visuals and presentation are the strongest suit, and it's full of charm. But ultimately I just felt it was a bit hollow and shallow on both sides of the game. The base building doesn't really feel like it has a way to do it right or wrong. You just build the stuff you unlock, make sure there's enough beds and sweep up the poop and make sure you cook every now and then. Not much to it, and you can automate more the further you get in.

The dungeon exploration is perfunctory. Small, The Binding of Isaac-esque levels to explore, with some item rooms you can get cards from (effectively buffs that last the run) and a couple of weapons. Weapon variety is limited (there's roughly 5 weapon types that can drop as normal, poison, vampiric, etc), a couple of spells that fit the usual archetypes (line cast, projectile, homing projectile, bomb) and combat is pretty simplistic stuff - hit and roll, cast here and there. Not bad, not amazing. It just does the job. 

The game maintains a solid feeling of progression and offers some interesting decisions to make as you unlock more rituals to perform for your cult (you pick between 2 every time you unlock a new ritual). But ultimately I just found it a bit simplistic. The cape mechanic where you can select an alternate cape for a buff/debuff is quite interesting but ultimately most of them don't make the drawbacks feel worthwhile apart from 1-2, and the game is easy enough with the regular cape that it didn't feel worth using anything other than the damage increasing one.

This game knocks it out of the park when it comes to the superficial - it's visually distinct and full of very crunchy and punchy effects.  The combination of combat-roguelike and colony sim is intriguing, and the game is absolutely effective at [i]drawing you in[/i]... much like any cult worth its salt strives to be.

Would that the similarities had ended there, but, also like a cult, a hollow existence awaits those who delve deeper into the game.  Every system introduced into this game, though many appear interesting at first, turns out to be disappointingly shallow.  The upgrades to buildings/tech offer little variety and are underwhelming in terms of any actual feeling of [i]progression[/i].  The combat upgrades are even less inspiring; you get new weapon types (insofar as just adding Poison or Crit to existing ones is [i]new[/i]), you get new spells (which I found unsatisfying to use), and there's little else worth mentioning.  These are arranged into a truly meager tree, with little apparent reason for its hierarchy and no sense of customization, since you must take nearly every option from one tier before advancing to the next.  Doctrines and Rituals are probably the most interesting systems, but these too lack depth, and don't feel very balanced or tuned for good pacing.

It feels strange to say about a game that, outwardly, seems so polished, but Cult of the Lamb felt almost [i]unfinished[/i].  It's not that you can see any gaping holes at a glance, and it's not that anything is evidently [i]broken[/i]... Rather, what's not done here is the expansion, evolution, and finishing touches that allow good ideas to mature and coalesce into great games.   It's as though there were a few solid brainstorming sessions, and the resulting high-level ideas were developed, arranged to look as enticing as possible, and released.  
With such excellent alternatives in the roguelike genre, it's hard not to feel that this approach is in some way a deliberate cash-grab rather than a true attempt to make a game the best it can be.

The shortcomings are not immediately apparent, and there are procedural obstacles (tiered trees and mandatory repeats of the same combat area) which do little other than extend playtime, so many who might've gone for a quick refund will remain enticed just long enough to make that impossible.  I wouldn't refund it myself, as I did have some genuine fun here, but the more I think about this game, the more a thumbs-down feels like a correct response.

Alright, that was the simple review, time for my detailed one. 
Ahem I'd recommend grabbing a snack. 

(This review is mainly for people looking to buy the game.)
(Some details are omitted for spoiler purposes)

Graphics: I personally adore the graphic style, it is not at all "realistic" if that is the style of games you're looking for. It's a game that has a "cartoony" vibe with dark undertones. Think, 2d platformer smashed with a 3d dungeon crawler then add some gore. It's a stylized look, as I'm sure you can tell from the pictures. There isn't much to say about the graphics besides they are awesome if you love tarot cards.

Gameplay: Personally I dont give a rats ass if the game is repetitive, if you dislike repetitive games DO NOT GET THIS GAME. I've seen reviews of people talking about how they HATE the gameplay loop. Allow me to describe the game loop to you quickly. 

Lamb (You) has a cult (Think animal crossing village), and to get materials, they need to leave the cult. Which is where the dungeon crawler comes in. 

You go through an area, get your materials, come back to the cult, build shit, then leave. 

Seems repetitive, which it is. However there are some things I glossed over like the fact you can leave the dungeon anytime (If you have the cloak for it, a cloak upgrade is basically when you defeat a big boss you get something to get a new cloak, and an ability of one of those cloaks is you can teleport out of the dungeon whenever you want with a short windup). So you're not "forced" to go through the full dungeon. Plus, I've actually seen people completely skip over the dungeon crawler portion, which I find kinda insane. The dungeon crawler is a key component of the game, but you CAN avoid it, HOWEVER it is SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult to deal with your cult.

 Basically what I'm stating here is: If you don't like dungeon crawlers this isn't the game for you, but if you love the game enough (stubborn enough) you could avoid that part of the game. You will be missing the story however so it's not recommended. 

Alright lets talk about the difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself now that everyone who hates dungeon crawlers has left. 

The difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself is player focused/skill. There are things that can assist, or make it more difficult for players either looking for a challenge or simplicity, which I will not get into much as that leads to spoilers. But lets simplify it, lets say you're just using vanilla lamb (basic/starter kit). Here's the basic dungeon rundown:

When you go into a dungeon, the dungeon will show multiple types of rooms. A dungeon run is called a CRUSADE. There's 14 total types of rooms. I would highly recommend searching “Cult Of The Lamb: Level Types” if you're a visual learner. I'll list all the rooms you'll come across keeping one out for spoiler purposes. If not, I'll try to explain here. The brackets are the symbols you'll see

Normal fight (Sword Symbol), Hearts (Heart), Coins (Coin), Food (The Food of that Dungeon), Lumber (Chopped Wood), Stone (Rocks), Bones (Crossbones), Tarot (Card), Shop (Shop), Event (Question Mark), New follower (Stick Figure Kneeling, Holding Hands upward), Miniboss (Skull and Crossbones). 

Okay Now ill briefly explain what each room actually IS;

Normal Fight: I will come back to this one to not confuse you

Hearts: You get Health

Coins: You get Money

Food: You get Food for your Cult

Lumber: You get Wood for your Cult

Stone: You get Stone for your Cult

Bones: You get Bones for your Cult 

Tarot: You get an NPC that gives you a temporary bonus ability ONLY for that run

Shop: You can buy shit there. Do you not know what a store is? Touch grass.

Event: This one basically has a chance of a few different rooms and I will avoid stating because of spoilers.


New Follower: You get the CHANCE to free a NPC to join your cult

Miniboss: This one will ONLY EVER appear at the end of the dungeon run. It is exactly as it's said. It's a miniboss. 

Alright now you know what rooms are congrats. Let's go back to the Normal Fight room. You will ALWAYS start a Crusade in a Normal Fight Room. A normal fight room is basically where you go through multiple smaller rooms freeroam (you get a minimap) and you fight shit. Make sure you explore everywhere because most of the time you have the chance of running into a Tarot type room, or an NPC, or Treasure. What's Treasure? Treasure can vary. Coins, Materials, or Weapons to use in the dungeon. During the start of the Crusade when you enter the Normal Fight Room you will get 2 weapons. A physical one, and a ranged one, and yes you carry this weapon throughout your entire crusade.

If your fucking confused. Think of a Russian nesting doll. There are the General levels, which I mentioned. Then the Normal Fight Rooms.

Okay enough about the gameplay, if you really need to know more search up a video stupid. 

Audio: The audio is heavenly, you just gotta hear it for yourself. Sadly the person who made the original music passed away. RIP your music was beautiful. 

PC Requirements: It's pretty average. You don't need a super computer, but you still have a decent computer. The size is workable, there really isn't much to talk about here, idk what computer you have. Figure it out yourself.

Grind: There isn't a grind. UNLESS you care about achievements. If you do, Well… have fun. 

Story: I will not go into the story at all as this is mostly a spoiler free review. However, the story is good, and the Final Boss Fight is awesome. Highly recommended.

Game Time: It gets repetitive, the game will go as long as you can go. 

Price: For me it's highly worth the price, and if you don't think so, just wait for it to go on sale. It goes on sale very often. I bought it full price, with every possible DLC. (Jumping on Woolhaven the second its OFFICIALLY out).

Bugs: Very Minor Bugs, If you do find any, report to the discord. They deal with it pretty quickly.

For me? 10/10 I love being a psychopathic lamb that runs a cult.


Thanks for reading my essay of a review, and I hope it helps you decide if you would be interested in the game or not! (RIP to my fingers)

Cult of the Lamb is a Great game. This is because it's two Good games bolted together.

Half the game is a short-run rogue-(very)-lite, with responsive gameplay where you go and fight varied bosses.
The other half is a lite town management game, where you have to keep people fed and faithful.

Both of them are fun, but not complex. The rogue-lite is 10 minute runs with one attack and one spell. There's a range of options there, but not a huge amount. This is not Binding of Isaac, even if it feels like a love letter to it's themes. 
The town management is something you are juggling in-between runs, keeping the faithful happy and unlocking new buildings that ease the strain of managing the town. They are cute and satisfying, but they are fairly simple and self-contained and don't require a lot of thought, while the aesthetic options suffer in that you are on an awkward diagonal grid which lessens the excitement of town design. This is not Planet Zoo, even if you can have one of every animal with the multitude of options.

The Woolhaven DLC adds some spice to the game, adding a bit more challenge to both the combat and the town management just when everything is starting to be a bit more routine and I think that part of the game is the highlight for me. Neither is really much more complex, but you can tell it's really been developed with Love.

So I stick with my rating that this is a Great game - provided you like both Rogue-lites AND Townbuilders. The big thing the game is bringing to you is the novelty of their fusion. If one of those genre's leaves you cold, you might be better served with one of the exemplars in that genre on their own.

Short version: "this game understands that Binding of Isaac did some good things, but not why it did them."

I played the game right through to the end. Took me about 15 hours. It has two halves, the city building simulator half where you construct stuff for your cult and the roguelite dungeon crawler where you fight through the lands of the corrupt Old Faith.

I would say the majority of the time I spent in this game was spent in the city builder half, simply because that's actually the part of the game that has the most negative consequences for failure; you actually need your cultists healthy and happy to level up your character. Once you get to a certain level of power - and it comes surprisingly quickly - the dungeon runs become trivial, but your cultists WILL starve or poop themselves to death if you leave them alone for too long. This counter-intuitively disincentivises you from exploring too much.

Basically, a lot of things in the cult settlement aren't automated that should be. For instance, followers can plant, water and fertilize crops after a few upgrades, but they can't harvest them until much later, and they can NEVER cook meals for themselves. Even once you get the upgrades, they'll plant seeds that you give them, but they'll never put seeds they retrieve after a harvest back into the seed bank; you have to do that yourself. You can build them outhouses so they don't stink the place up pooping in the bushes, but they'll never clean out the outhouses and transport the poop to the fertilizer silo. You always have to do that yourself.

The city-building is both very labour intensive but also very shallow. I feel like I'm doing a lot of busywork, collecting things and putting things in places in a way that should be automated. I'm leading a cult, for gods' sake, can't I just tell a follower to cook me a meal? The settlement half's need for constant attention seems to clash with the dungeon crawling half. It's quite telling that one of the abilities you unlock quite early in the game is the ability to just teleport home while out dungeon crawling to deal with settlement crises.

But the dungeon crawling half is where things get... really weird. Comparisons with Binding of Isaac are very warranted, because the game is notable both in what it copies and what it doesn't copy, and how that changes the experience.

The game straight-up lifts Binding of Isaac's red/blue/black hearts system with essentially no change whatsoever. Red hearts leave empty containers when depleted, blue hearts vanish, and black hearts vanish after doing damage to everything in the room. Binding of Isaac had a maddeningly specific meta as to which type of heart was more useful in a given situation, and learning it was a key part of skill progression. 

In Cult of the Lamb you always play the character and there essentially aren't any passive items, so there's almost no meta. The only thing that differentiates the hearts at all is that black hearts deal damage when you lose them. Since there are no equivalent to Devil Deals and there doesn't seem to be much consequence to losing red hearts, there's no longer a meaningful distinction between them. Blue hearts drop just about as often as red hearts do. They still go "in front" of red hearts, but that doesn't seem to mean anything anymore.

The core gameplay IS a bit different to Binding of Isaac - your attacks are melee, and you can dodge roll. Enemy attacks are telegraphed, although how well varies by enemy. Your weapons go dagger, sword, claw, axe and hammer, each being slower but more damaging than the last. There are various spells that give you ranged options, or a more damaging melee attack. You start with a small selection, but can unlock more through progressing your settlement, and you can also raise the level of the weapons you are randomly assigned at the start of a run.

This random assignment is another issue. If you get a hammer but don't like the way the hammer works? Tough, either go home and start the run again, or deal with it. I don't like this at all. This is a bad application of RNG. This is another thing that CotL has lifted from BoI and tried to apply without actually understanding what it did or why: Binding of Isaac had random item drops on non-random characters. You always chose your character and this to some degree determined their playstyle. You generally knew roughly what you wanted to be doing when you chose a specific character - what sort of items you wanted to pick up or not, what tarot cards you'd use or not use, how exactly you'd approach fighting, etc.

When I start the game in Cult of the Lamb and it offers me either a dagger (very fast attacks but pitiful damage and a lower attack range than other weapons) or the hammer (crushing AoE attacks but with a massive attack delay) I just want to restart the run. What's maddening is that at the very end of the game, just before the final boss, it offers you a much larger array of possible weapons to choose from, almost as if the devs KNEW that the random weapon assignment was going to mess with players.

The dungeons themselves are *very* small and *very* linear - usually small clusters of 9-10 rooms, separated from each other by a map screen that sometimes offers you single-room set pieces instead of a dungeon layer. Overall, the dungeon crawling feels very shallow in comparison to BoI which it's clearly trying to emulate. 

What's frustrating is that despite this, the dungeon crawling is the only part of the game that doesn't feel almost calculated to waste your time.

As previously mentioned, other than its weapons and spells, the game has no random item drops, so you don't really have the fun of making incredibly weird or broken builds like in Binding of Isaac. There is a tarot card system that gives you passive buffs, but most of the tarot cards are locked at the start of the game. To unlock them, you have to build up your settlement and do quests for various NPCs you find in the wilderness or in other nearby settlements. There's a variety of minigames and quests associated with this. These sidequests and minigames are usually not bad on their own, but they split your attention even more ways between the city building and dungeon crawling.

Every time you pick up a blueprint or tarot card, there is a LONG animation sequence - at least 5 to 10 seconds. Remember how in Starfox Adventures, there was that 17-second long, unskippable animation and fanfare whenever you picked up an item? It's like that. Acquiring Devotion from the shrine at the centre of your settlement requires you to hold down a mouse button or key on your keyboard for anywhere up to 30 seconds. I can't envision a situation in which I'd EVER want to NOT take all the devotion at once. It doesn't decay once you hold it. There's also certain situations where when you're depositing or withdrawing items from a building, you can't even hold down a button: you have to click it repeatedly.

All in all, the game is a shallow, frustratingly labour-intensive city builder that actively gets in the way of the shallow, frustratingly random dungeon crawler, painted over with some truly excellent writing and graphic design and some passable music and sound design. I don't think it's impossible to merge city building with roguelite dungeon crawling, I just don't think this game did it elegantly. I enjoyed this game a little bit, but not enough to justify what I paid for it.

[h1][b]Cult of the Lamb[/b][/h1]
[i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] is a cute action roguelike / roguelite, adventure game in which the player starts a cult and slays non-believers whilst caring for their own cult members. 

[b]Story[/b]

The story of [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] is quite straightforward: The Lamb, who is the protagonist of this cute action-adventure roguelike, is being sacrificed but gets rescued by “The One Who Waits” – a strange and mysterious deity who tasks the Lamb to start their own cult and start to slay all non-believers.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2851438911
[b]Personal Note[/b]

When Massive Monster showed their first teaser for [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] I was quite intrigued to see what they could pull off with such an interesting indie title. After it being hyped up during the Devolver Digital Showcase 2022, the demo was around the corner and I immediately felt like [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] is a neat game.

Gameplay wise the player manages a cult that slowly grows larger and larger. Besides managing the cult, the player goes on so called “crusades” that are essentially roguelike encounters in which the player slays a bunch of different enemies until reaching a minor, and later one, a bigger boss.

Managing the cult isn’t as tedious as it might seem, but remembering to do sermons every in-game day to get more powerful quickly, could feel a bit tedious at times. 

While managing your cult you can establish doctrines that push some pro and cons into your playthrough which makes building your own cult a bit more complex than it looks at first.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2985210071
The progression system is bound to sermons that are being influenced by how many members are taking part in those sermons. The more members take part in it, the faster the player will unlock more passive advantages for the roguelike element of the game. Later on, after defeating each major boss, the player will get more upgrades that will help during the crusades. Unlocking buildings for the cult itself works similar.

Is there any replayability? I’d say yeah there is, since after defeating any major boss the player will be able to run those crusades infinitely, or as long as the player wants to. There is a bunch of collectibles and achievements as well, which helps with the replayability of [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i].

Besides some minor things like: placing floor tiles being a bit wonky when using mouse & keyboard, there are not many negative things about the game itself. The only thing that comes to mind is that the game is probably completable in about 14 hours, that’s just killing all bosses and getting most, if not all, upgrades for the Lamb and important buildings for the cult itself.

[i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] has probably one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard and they perfectly fit to the game and its vibe.

[b]Rating[/b]
[list][b]Pros[/b]
[*] Nice narrative
[*] Unique-ish combination of genres
[*] Great visuals and cute aesthetics  
[*] Awesome soundtrack
[*] Good voice acting
[/list]
[list][b]Cons[/b]
[*] A bit short
[*] Difficulty settings need some work
[/list]
[b]Conclusion[/b] 

Is [i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] worth your money? I’d say: Yeah it is.

It’s a nice and cute little action-adventure game that has roguelike / roguelite elements in it and offers managing a cult with followers, building stuff as well as collecting things – so there is a lot to do in a game that is technically beatable in roughly 14 hours.

[i]Cult of the Lamb[/i] is a neat but not perfect game and it’s honestly worth your money if you like the genres.

[b]8.4 / 10[/b]
